metadata.title: A clinical-ultrasound nomogram for predicting central lymph node metastasis in C-TIRADS 4 thyroid nodules: A retrospective cohort study

sections.text: To address the clinical bottleneck in preoperative assessment of central lymph node metastasis (CLNM) in patients with C-TIRADS (Chinese Thyroid Imaging Reporting And Data System) 4 papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), this study aims to develop a preoperative predictive model capable of quantifying individual metastasis risk through integrated multifactorial analysis, thereby guiding more precise surgical planning. A retrospective analysis was conducted on the clinical-pathological characteristics and ultrasound features of 196 patients with C-TIRADS 4 PTC who underwent thyroid surgery at the Lequn Campus of the First Hospital of Jilin University between January 2021 and December 2023. Univariate and multivariate binary logistic regression analyses were employed to identify independent risk factors for CLNM. The diagnostic performance of the predictive model was evaluated, and a nomogram was developed to forecast the risk of thyroid cancer metastasis. This study included a total of 196 patients, with a CLNM incidence rate of 47.45%. Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that age < 55 years ( P = .024), multiple nodules ( P = .033), nodular borders with poor definition ( P = .001), microcalcifications ( P = .002), very hypoechoic ( P = .041), and capsular contact ( P < .001) were independent risk factors for CLNM. The established logistic regression model for diagnosing CLNM yielded an AUC of 0.791, with sensitivity and specificity of 62.4% and 82.5%, respectively. This study developed a nomogram for predicting thyroid cancer metastasis risk based on retrospective data, integrating 6 independent predictors: patient age, number of lesions, margin characteristic, microcalcification, very hypoechoic, and capsular contact. The predictive model demonstrated good performance for predicting CLNM.

In recent years, the incidence of PTC has shown a rising trend, ranking seventh among all cancers in 2022. [ 1 ] The reasons for this trend may be related to the increased use of thyroid ultrasound and the application of new imaging technologies. Among these, PTC is the most common pathological type, accounting for 85% of all thyroid cancer cases. [ 2 ] Research demonstrates that although PTC has a low mortality rate and favorable prognosis, CLNM significantly increases disease recurrence rates and treatment complexity. A meta-analysis involving 9369 patients revealed a cervical lymph node metastasis rate of 37.17% in PTC. [ 3 ] And according to statistics, the incidence rate of CLNM among patients can reach 24.1% to 64.1%. [ 4 ] Although ultrasound offers certain advantages in examining cervical lymph nodes, its sensitivity for detecting CLNM in PTC is relatively low, at only 33%, and it also faces challenges in visualizing normal central lymph nodes, and cannot detect occult lymph node metastasis. [ 5 ] Research has confirmed that prophylactic clearance of central lymph nodes in patients can reduce the recurrence rate of PTC, but it increases the risk of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism. [ 6 ] Therefore, preoperative confirmation of the status of cervical lymph nodes is crucial. C-TIRADS classifies thyroid nodules by malignant risk, with C-TIRADS 4 nodules (including 4A, 4B, and 4C) carrying a malignant risk ranging from 2% to 90%. This category encompasses nodules ranging from likely benign to highly suspicious for malignancy, serving as a key classification system for managing thyroid nodules in China. [ 7 ] However, C-TIRADS 4 nodules present greater diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to their wide range of malignant risk and the intermingling of malignant and benign features. Particularly in cases already diagnosed as PTC, the CLNM status directly influences surgical approach selection and prognosis assessment. Concurrently, some C-TIRADS 4 nodules may harbor occult metastases. Yet, due to their relatively low malignant risk, there remains no clear consensus on whether active intervention is warranted. While category 5 nodules possess numerous malignant features, category 4 nodules have a lower probability of presenting these features. Previous prediction models based on “all PTCs” were likely dominated conclusions drawn from a large number of typical category 5 nodules. When physicians encounter an “atypical” category 4 nodule, the guidance value of these models may diminish. Our core hypothesis is that within the complex group of C-TIRADS 4 nodules, there exists a unique set of ultrasound and clinical features that can effectively predict lymph node metastasis. Therefore, this study focuses on patients with postoperative pathologically confirmed PTC who were classified as C-TIRADS 4 preoperatively. By systematically analyzing their preoperative ultrasound imaging features and clinicopathological data, we aim to identify risk factors independently associated with CLNM, and subsequently construct and validate a clinical model specifically designed to predict the risk of CLNM in this patient population.

This study employed a retrospective cohort design and consecutively enrolled patients who underwent surgical treatment for thyroid cancer at the Lequn Campus of the First Hospital of Jilin University between January 2021 and December 2023. Inclusion criteria were: Patients undergoing initial thyroid surgery at our hospital (including total thyroidectomy, subtotal thyroidectomy, lobectomy, etc) with at least central neck lymph node dissection; No prior treatment received before surgery; Preoperative thyroid ultrasound examination performed at our hospital with clear nodule imaging preserved; Ultrasound report indicating C-TIRADS 4 nodules; Postoperative pathology report confirming the presence of CLNM. Exclusion criteria included: Recurrent PTC or other types of thyroid cancer; Metastatic thyroid cancer or concomitant malignancies in other sites; Patients with distant metastasis; Patients without central zone lymph node dissection; Patients with incomplete clinical data; Patients with a history of head and neck radiation or a family history of thyroid cancer. This study has been approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Jilin University. Ultrasound examinations are performed by experienced sonographers using internationally recognized high-resolution color Doppler ultrasound diagnostic systems. These include the Philips IU22 and EPIQ5 models equipped with 5–12MHz linear array probes, as well as the GE LOGIQ E9 device featuring 6–15MHz linear array probes. Throughout all examinations, patients are positioned in a standard supine position without a pillow, with the neck fully extended to maximize exposure of the examination area. The examination follows a systematic scanning protocol, employing high-frequency linear probes to perform meticulous multi-planar, multi-angle scans of the thyroid gland. Surgical procedures encompass corresponding techniques including local excision of thyroid nodules, unilateral thyroid lobectomy, unilateral thyroid lobectomy with isthmus resection, near-total thyroidectomy, subtotal thyroidectomy, and total thyroidectomy. All cases routinely underwent at least central neck lymph node dissection. Postoperative pathological diagnosis served as the gold standard. Final pathology reports for all patients were retrieved from our hospital’s electronic medical record database to ensure data integrity and accuracy.

Retrospective collection of patient gender and age information from the medical record system. Acquisition of patient tumor count, presence of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and CLNM status from pathology reports. Ultrasound characteristics include tumor size (maximum diameter of a single nodule; in cases with multiple suspicious nodules within the thyroid, the maximum diameter of the largest nodule is selected, and ultrasound characteristics are assessed for that largest nodule). Ultrasound feature analysis was performed by 2 sonographers with over 5 years of experience, blinded to pathological results. In cases of disagreement, they reached a consensus through discussion. Each case required assessment of the following ultrasound features: nodule margin, shape, aspect ratio, internal echo pattern, presence of microcalcifications, capsular contact and the presence of blood flow signals within the nodule on color Doppler imaging.

All data were statistically analyzed using SPSS version 26.0 and R software version 4.4.1. Univariate binary logistic regression analysis was performed with clinical-pathological and ultrasound characteristics as independent variables and the pathological outcome of CLNM occurrence as the dependent variable to identify relevant factors for CLNM. Variables with P < .10 in univariate logistic regression were selected as independent variables for multivariate binary logistic regression analysis with CLNM occurrence as the dependent variable to determine independent risk factors for CLNM in PTC. Statistical significance was set at P < .05. Subsequently, based on the results of the multivariate analysis, a predictive nomogram was constructed using the rms package in R to visually represent the model and provide an individualized risk estimation tool.

This study included 196 patients diagnosed with PTC through postoperative pathological examination, comprising 160 females and 36 males. Patient ages ranged from 21 to 72 years, with a mean age of (45.9 ± 10.2) years; 19.39% of patients were aged ≥ 55 years. Tumor sizes ranged from 2.5 to 60.0 mm, with a mean size of (12.5 ± 10.1) mm. Among these, 43.37% of nodules were ≥ 1 cm. Additionally, the CLNM rate in this study was 47.45% (Table 1 ), and the CLNM rate increased with higher C-TIRADS classifications (Table 2 ).

sections.section: 3.2. Association Between Clnm And Clinical-Pathological Characteristics
sections.text: To identify risk factors for CLNM metastasis, we performed univariate binary logistic regression analysis on the clinical-pathological characteristics and ultrasound features of all patients. Univariate analysis revealed statistically significant differences between the CLNM group and the non-CLNM group in nodule size ( P < .001), number of nodules ( P = .042), nodule shape ( P = .033), nodule boundary ( P = .002), presence of microcalcifications ( P < .001), and thyroid capsular contact ( P < .001) (Table 3 ). In contrast, no significant association was observed between CLNM and the presence of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis ( P = .678). Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed on variables with P < .10 in the univariate analysis. Results indicated that patient age < 55 years (OR = 2.723, 95% CI: 1.140–6.505, P = .024), multiple nodules (OR = 0.741, 95% CI: 1.064–4.142, P = .033), nodular borders with indistinct margins (OR = 3.016, 95% CI: 1.530–5.945, P = .001), and nodules with microcalcifications (OR = 3.080, 95% CI: 1.528–6.209, P = .002), nodules with very hypoechoic appearance (OR = 2.070, 95% CI: 1.029–4.164, P = .041), and nodule contact with the thyroid capsule (OR = 4.794, 95% CI: 2.282–10.070, P < .001) were independent risk factors for CLNM occurrence in PTC (Table 4 ). The ROC curve indicates that the regression model demonstrates an AUC of 0.791 (95% CI: 0.782–0.853) for diagnosing CLNM, with sensitivity and specificity of 62.4% and 82.5%, respectively, reflecting significant discriminatory capability (Fig. 1 ). Furthermore, the independent predictors identified through multivariate logistic regression analysis were utilized to construct a prediction nomogram (Fig. 2 ). This graph visually displays the scoring criteria for each variable and its contribution to the risk of metastasis. By summing the scores of all variables to obtain a total score, the individual patient’s probability of metastasis can be directly read on.

In recent years, the incidence of thyroid cancer has been gradually increasing, with PTC being the most common type. CLNM not only significantly increases the risk of disease recurrence but also influences the choice of surgical approach and the patient’s long-term prognosis. Currently, there remains controversy over whether prophylactic central lymph node dissection (PCLND) should be performed for all PTC patients. PCLND helps reduce postoperative recurrence rates but may also increase surgery-related complications such as hypocalcemia and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. Therefore, accurately predicting CLNM preoperatively holds significant clinical value. Although previous studies have extensively analyzed factors associated with CLNM in PTC, few have specifically investigated LNM characteristics in C-TIRADS 4 nodules. This retrospective study analyzed the clinical-pathological and ultrasound characteristics of C-TIRADS 4 PTC patients to identify risk factors for CLNM. The significance of C-TIRADS 4 nodules in predicting CLNM risk cannot be overlooked. This study indicates that LNM occurrence in C-TIRADS 4 patients remains influenced by patient age < 55 years, multiple nodules, ill-defined nodule margins, microcalcifications within nodules, very hypoechoic and nodule contact with the thyroid capsule. This suggests that relying solely on C-TIRADS classification cannot accurately predict CLNM. Clinical assessment should integrate high-risk ultrasound features with other independent risk factors for comprehensive evaluation to optimize surgical decision-making. Although C-TIRADS 4 nodules appear “milder” than category 5 on ultrasound, their CLNM risk remains substantial, potentially due to the higher aggressiveness of some 4C nodules. Despite not fully meeting C-TIRADS 5 criteria, these nodules exhibit features such as multiplicity, microcalcifications, and ill-defined borders, suggesting more aggressive biological behavior. Notably, the incidence of CLNM progressively increases with higher C-TIRADS grades, reaching 60.5% for 4C nodules in this study. Furthermore, ROC curve analysis demonstrated that the established logistic regression model exhibits good diagnostic performance for predicting CLNM (AUC = 0.791), indicating that combined multifactorial prediction enhances diagnostic accuracy. Age is a significant factor influencing CLNM in PTC, studies indicate that the incidence of CLNM gradually decreases with increasing age. [ 8 ] Different studies define the age threshold differently, such as Paritosh et al [ 9 ] believed that < 45 years of age is associated with CLNM, while Xu et al [ 10 ] noted that age ≤ 36 years is an independent risk factor, though the overall trend remains consistent. This study set the age threshold at 55 years, aligning with the new thyroid TNM staging system classification, and similarly found a higher incidence of CLNM in younger patients. Gene expression analysis revealed differences in gene expression among PTC patients across different age groups, suggesting that age may have a molecular basis for influencing CLNM. [ 11 ] Additionally, younger patients have higher metabolic rates and faster tumor progression, which may increase the risk of cervical lymph node metastasis. [ 12 ] Multifocality is a common feature of PTC, occurring in approximately 18% to 87% of cases. It is recognized as an independent risk factor for CLNM, with the risk of CLNM increasing in parallel with the number of nodules. [ 13 – 15 ] Research indicates that PTC cancer cells may metastasize via the intraglandular lymphatic network, leading to increased multifocal tumor invasiveness and thereby elevating the risk of cervical lymph node metastasis. [ 16 ] Additionally, multifocality may arise from either a single clonal origin or the independent development of distinct clones, with the proliferation of mutated clones enhancing their capacity for proliferation and metastasis. [ 17 , 18 ] Additionally, multifocality is closely associated with recurrence following PTC surgery, necessitating particular attention during preoperative assessment. [ 19 ] This study confirms that nodule contact with the thyroid capsule is an independent risk factor for CLNM, consistent with findings from some previous studies. [ 20 ] Furthermore, contact with the capsule exhibits the strongest association with CLNM. The mechanism may involve tumor cells becoming more prone to invading surrounding tissues after breaching the capsule, thereby increasing the risk of lymph node metastasis. [ 21 ] Microcalcifications are a characteristic ultrasound feature of PTC and are closely associated with tumor invasiveness and CLNM. [ 22 ] It may indicate a higher risk of metastasis by reflecting rapid tumor growth and active cell proliferation. [ 23 ] Additionally, ill-defined margins may serve as an independent risk factor for CLNM, typically indicating tumor infiltration into surrounding tissues, which may increase the risk of metastasis. [ 24 ] Extremely low echogenicity refers to thyroid nodules exhibiting echogenicity lower than the presternal pectoralis muscles, presenting as markedly hypoechoic. This study identifies extremely low echogenicity as an independent risk factor for CLNM. Findings confirm that nodular fibrosis exceeding 30% is independently associated with extremely low echogenicity, potentially due to reduced echogenic interfaces and diminished acoustic reflection caused by dense fibrosis. [ 25 ] Moreover, some scholars believe that fibrosis in PTC is associated with lymph node or distant metastasis. [ 26 ] Lim et al [ 27 ] also noted that tumors exhibiting extremely low echogenicity preoperatively may demonstrate higher invasiveness. The findings of this study hold significant implications for clinical practice, particularly regarding the preoperative assessment and management of C-TIRADS 4 nodules. The study revealed a higher incidence of CLNM in category 4C nodules. Therefore, preoperative evaluation should comprehensively consider high-risk ultrasound features, tumor size, capsular contact, and imaging characteristics to optimize surgical strategies. For patients exhibiting high-risk features such as microcalcifications or capsular involvement, heightened vigilance for CLNM is warranted. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) or additional imaging studies may be indicated to determine the necessity of prophylactic central lymph node dissection. Conversely, low-risk C-TIRADS 4 patients may be managed with close follow-up to avoid overtreatment. Furthermore, this study indicates varying CLNM rates within the C-TIRADS 4 category. Future research may refine CLNM risk prediction models for different subcategories, thereby enhancing the clinical utility of C-TIRADS in preoperative assessment. The limitations of this study include its retrospective design and relatively small sample size, which precluded analysis of specific risk factors for CLNM across individual grades. Second, due to the retrospective design of this study, real-time observation of the ultrasound features of thyroid nodules was not possible, which may have affected the accuracy of nodule scoring. Additionally, thyroid function and autoantibody parameters and molecular biological indicators such as gene mutations were not incorporated. Future research could explore the genetic characteristics of C-TIRADS 4 nodules to further optimize CLNM risk prediction models. Additionally, ultrasound assessment inherently involves some degree of subjectivity. Although double-blind evaluation was employed to minimize bias in this study, it may still affect the stability of the results. Future multi-center, large-sample prospective studies could further validate the clinical utility of this model and integrate new technologies like artificial intelligence to enhance preoperative prediction methods for CLNM.

In summary, through systematic analysis, this study not only clearly identified independent risk factors for CLNM in C-TIRADS 4 PTC patients but also successfully constructed and validated an individualized prediction nomogram integrating these factors. This model demonstrates excellent discrimination and calibration, translating multimodal preoperative information into an intuitive, quantifiable personal risk score. It provides critical decision support for clinicians to accurately identify high-risk patients preoperatively and tailor surgical dissection plans. This study fills a gap in refined risk assessment tools for the specific C-TIRADS 4 population. Future external validation through multicenter, prospective studies will advance its translation and application into clinical practice.
